nodes.label: A lock protects an invariant, not a statement
nodes.rationale: Locking only the write is pointless because the stale value was already read. The critical section must span every step that assumes the balance has not changed — ask 'what am I assuming stays true?' and lock that whole span.

nodes.label: Lock granularity: global vs per-account vs per-field
nodes.rationale: Granularity is the dial between correctness and throughput. One global lock is correct but serialises the whole bank; per-field is fastest but makes deadlock very likely. Per-entity (per account, via ConcurrentDictionary<Guid, SemaphoreSlim>) is the sweet spot: only same-account requests queue.

nodes.label: SemaphoreSlim rather than lock
nodes.rationale: You cannot await inside a lock block: a monitor is owned by the thread that entered it, and an await may resume on a different thread that would release a lock it never took. SemaphoreSlim(1,1) is owned by nobody so any continuation can release it. The cost is no reentrancy and no ownership — every acquire needs exactly one release, guarded here by Interlocked.Exchange because a double release raises the count and silently admits two actors.

nodes.label: Never hold a lock across I/O you don't control
nodes.rationale: Pessimistic coordination converts other people's latency into your own. If the critical section calls an external provider taking 2 seconds, every other request for that account waits 2 seconds. Do the slow call outside the lock and re-validate inside it.

nodes.label: In-process lock: correct on one instance, silently broken on three
nodes.rationale: The semaphore dictionary is a field on one object in one process. Three replicas hold three separate semaphores for the same account id, so there is no mutual exclusion at all — the lost update returns with code that looks correct. This is the hinge of the whole repo; the strategy reports scalesAcrossInstances:false. The fix is not a better lock but moving coordination to shared state (database or distributed lock) behind the same IAccountLock interface.

nodes.label: xmin as an EF Core concurrency token
nodes.rationale: xmin is a PostgreSQL system column holding the id of the transaction that last wrote the row; Postgres bumps it on every UPDATE for free, so it is a version counter with zero schema cost and no code to maintain. Marked IsConcurrencyToken() EF appends it to the UPDATE WHERE clause; zero rows matched raises DbUpdateConcurrencyException. Advantage over an application-maintained Version column: raw SQL outside EF still bumps it.

nodes.label: Bounded retry loop with re-read and re-decide
nodes.rationale: Three things are easy to get wrong: a fresh DbContext per attempt (reusing one keeps the stale entity tracked so the retry re-sends the same doomed UPDATE forever), re-reading AND re-deciding rather than just re-sending the write, and bounding the retries. Unbounded retry under heavy contention is a livelock — everything busy, nothing progressing. Jittered exponential backoff belongs in production.

nodes.label: Optimistic concurrency pays in wasted work
nodes.rationale: Measured: 5 actors, 9 attempts, 4 conflicts, 0.0 ms waited. Nobody blocks anybody; the price of a collision is rework. It degrades under contention by doing N× the work for 1× the throughput rather than by corrupting data — a better failure mode, but still a failure mode, and one that only appears under load.

nodes.label: The hot row
nodes.rationale: One account everyone hits, a global counter, a shared inventory row. Every write conflicts with every other, so optimistic concurrency retry-storms. That is the signal to switch to pessimistic locking or to redesign the row so it stops being hot.

nodes.label: SELECT *, xmin ... FOR UPDATE row lock
nodes.rationale: Three things make it correct: it is inside a transaction (a row lock lives until the transaction ends), the read is inside the lock, and the lock is held until commit so no check-to-write window exists. xmin must be named explicitly because a system column is not returned by SELECT *. SQL Server equivalent is WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK).

nodes.label: Pessimistic concurrency pays in waiting
nodes.rationale: Measured on identical input: 5 attempts, 0 conflicts, 244.1 ms waited versus optimistic's 9 attempts, 4 conflicts, 0.0 ms. Conflicts are prevented rather than detected, so nothing is redone — but total wall time is the sum of the queue, not the max.

nodes.label: Connection pool exhaustion from blocked transactions
nodes.rationale: Every blocked transaction holds a connection. Enough waiters and unrelated endpoints start failing — one of the most common causes of 'the database is down' incidents that turn out not to be the database's fault. Related failure modes: long transactions and SQL Server lock escalation.

nodes.label: Serializable isolation is optimistic in character
nodes.rationale: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE is explicit locking, mostly orthogonal to isolation level (Postgres defaults to Read Committed). Serializable would also prevent the lost update, but by aborting transactions with a serialization failure — so you need a retry loop again, and it serialises more than intended.

nodes.label: Conflict rate is the deciding variable
nodes.rationale: The question is not which is better but how often two people collide on the same row. Order-of-magnitude guidance: under 1% optimistic comfortably; 1-10% optimistic with bounded retries and jittered backoff; over 10% pessimistic, or redesign so the hot row stops being hot. Naming the deciding variable is what an interviewer listens for; 'optimistic, always' loses.

nodes.label: The optimistic/pessimistic crossover point
nodes.rationale: At low contention optimistic wins easily — lock-free throughput, almost nothing conflicts. At high contention pessimistic wins because optimistic's retries multiply work while throughput stays flat. Where the crossover sits depends on transaction length and conflict rate, so measure rather than guess.

nodes.label: The cheapest concurrency control is needing none
nodes.rationale: If the whole operation fits in one SQL statement — UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 40 WHERE id = ? AND balance >= 40 — the database does read-decide-write atomically and there is no gap to coordinate. Reach for this first; tokens and locks are for logic that does not fit.

nodes.label: Redesigning so the hot row stops being hot
nodes.rationale: Four moves that remove the contention rather than manage it: shard the counter across N rows summed on read, queue the writes and apply them serially, event-source by appending immutable events that cannot conflict, and batch many changes into one transaction.

nodes.label: Both strategies look identical in testing
nodes.rationale: With one user there are no conflicts, so optimistic never retries and pessimistic never waits. The difference appears only under concurrency, which is exactly when experimenting is hardest. This is why the lab forces the race and why forceRace:false exists — to show how rarely the problem surfaces by chance, and therefore how easily it reaches production.

nodes.label: The four Coffman conditions
nodes.rationale: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait must all hold. Mutual exclusion is the point of locking and cannot go; the database supplies preemption by killing a victim; breaking the circular wait is nearly always the right fix because it costs one comparison and no throughput.

nodes.label: Ordered lock acquisition
nodes.rationale: Sort the two account ids and always lock the lower first, so every transaction reaches for the same account first and no cycle can form. The order is arbitrary — it only has to be consistent; primary key is stable and needs no coordination. Generalises to any number of locks. The catch is that it is a convention nothing enforces: one new code path locking in a different order reintroduces the bug, and deadlocks form between code paths, not within one method.

nodes.label: Postgres deadlock detection (SQLSTATE 40P01)
nodes.rationale: PostgreSQL detects the cycle and kills one transaction, rolling its work back entirely — a deadlock costs a failed request, not corruption, and is safe to retry with bounded jittered backoff on 40P01 only (SQL Server 1205). In-process SemaphoreSlim cycles get no such favour: they hang forever with no detection, which is a real argument for pushing coordination into the database.

nodes.label: Livelock
nodes.rationale: A deadlock is stuck doing nothing; a livelock is busy achieving nothing — actors politely retrying forever, each backing off into the other. Optimistic concurrency's retry storm is the livelock risk, which is why lesson 03's retries are bounded.

nodes.label: Starvation
nodes.rationale: A third failure mode: one actor keeps losing while others progress. Common with optimistic retries under load, where the unlucky actor is always last. Fairness — a queue — fixes it; retries do not.

nodes.label: Make the timing a parameter, not an accident
nodes.rationale: With holdBetweenLocksMs at 0 the two transactions often do not overlap and no deadlock occurs — which is exactly what makes deadlocks hard to catch in testing. Widening the window makes the failure reliable, the same trick as the interleaving gate in lesson 01, and the test asserts the fix across five consecutive runs because a fix for an intermittent bug has to be proven repeatedly.

nodes.label: Per-item synchronisation makes parallel slower than sequential
nodes.rationale: 400,000 items means 400,000 lock acquisitions through a single door every core must pass. Measured 164.25 ms against 18.36 ms sequential (0.11x), and 11.09x the sequential baseline in BenchmarkDotNet. ConcurrentQueue is worse still at 0.13x with 2 MB allocated — a concurrent collection is thread-safe, not fast, and is not an aggregation strategy.

nodes.label: Partition the work, aggregate at the end
nodes.rationale: Parallel.For with localInit/localFinally accumulates privately per worker and merges about four times instead of 400,000, giving 3.68x on 4 cores — near-linear. PLINQ does the same declaratively at 2.84x and should be preferred for readability without a measured reason otherwise. How you aggregate matters more than whether you parallelise: the spread between fastest and slowest strategy is 33x with all six using every core.

nodes.label: False sharing
nodes.rationale: Interlocked per item (0.52x) is better than a lock — one atomic instruction rather than a synchronisation primitive — but still slower than sequential because all cores hammer one memory location and each write invalidates that cache line in the other cores' caches. Symptom: correct, parallel, and slower than expected.

nodes.label: Amdahl's law
nodes.rationale: If 10% of a job is inherently sequential then even infinite cores cap the speedup at 10x. Combined with memory bandwidth and cache limits, this is why 3.68x on 4 cores is a good result rather than a disappointment.

nodes.label: Preconditions for parallelism paying off
nodes.rationale: All four are required: genuinely CPU-bound work, enough items to cover partitioning and scheduling, expensive enough per item, and independent items. On a busy web server the server is already using every core serving requests, so parallelising one request steals from another — set MaxDegreeOfParallelism or move the work to a batch job.

nodes.label: Parallel.ForEach with an async lambda is async void
nodes.rationale: Parallel.ForEach takes Action<T>, so an async lambda becomes fire-and-forget with unobservable exceptions and returns before the work finishes. Use Parallel.ForEachAsync (.NET 6+).

nodes.label: await inside a loop serialises independent calls
nodes.rationale: Each iteration waits for the previous one, so ten independent 200 ms calls take 2005 ms for no reason. The code is genuinely asynchronous — it releases the thread — it is just needlessly serialised. Async and concurrent are not the same thing, and this is one of the most common .NET performance bugs because it looks completely correct.

nodes.label: Task.WhenAll fan-out
nodes.rationale: Select(...) starts each task; WhenAll launches nothing, it waits for things already in flight. Total time becomes the slowest call rather than the sum — 2005 ms to 204 ms. Beware .Select(async …) over a lazy IEnumerable enumerated twice; .ToArray() before awaiting to fix when the tasks started.

nodes.label: await releases threads rather than creating them
nodes.rationale: await Task.Delay registers a continuation and returns the thread to the pool, so ten in-flight waits cost roughly zero threads — the five observed are just whichever pool threads resumed continuations. Thread.Sleep holds its thread. At 1,000 concurrent requests each waiting 100 ms, blocking needs ~1,000 threads at ~1 MB of stack each; async needs a handful. That difference is the entire value of async on a server.

nodes.label: Throttled fan-out with SemaphoreSlim
nodes.rationale: Unbounded WhenAll over 10,000 items fires 10,000 simultaneous calls and moves your outage to your dependency. Cap it with a SemaphoreSlim, releasing in a finally — an exception that skipped the release permanently shrinks the pool, a slow-motion deadlock that looks like the service getting gradually slower. Measured: 10 checks at concurrency 4 is 3 batches x 200 ms = 603 ms, slower than unbounded on purpose. Parallel.ForEachAsync does the same with less code.

nodes.label: Task.Run is not how you make something async
nodes.rationale: Wrapping a blocking call hides the blocking, it does not remove it, and on a server you now occupy two threads instead of one. Measured at 1,857x slower than the direct call for trivial synchronous work, allocating 1.36 MB. Async has to go all the way down. Task.Run is legitimate only for getting genuinely CPU-bound work off the request thread — and even then a background job may be the better home.

nodes.label: ValueTask on hot synchronous-completion paths
nodes.rationale: async ValueTask always-completed measured at 13.0 µs and zero allocation against async Task's 128.3 µs and 720 KB. It earns its keep on hot paths that usually complete synchronously — a cache hit, a buffered read — but it can only be awaited once, so misusing it is worse than the allocation it saves.

nodes.label: CancellationToken propagation
nodes.rationale: Threading the token through every async method is tedious and is the difference between a client disconnect freeing resources immediately and the server working on answers nobody will read. ASP.NET Core supplies the request's token for free.

nodes.label: Scaling is three questions: code, instances, data
nodes.rationale: Interviewers rarely say which of the three they mean, and the order matters. Kubernetes multiplies instances; it cannot make un-scalable code scalable. The senior closer is refusing to touch any layer before knowing which one is actually the problem — most 'we need to scale' turns out to be one N+1 query.

nodes.label: Thread-pool starvation from sync-over-async
nodes.rationale: Measured with 100 virtual users for 10 s on a 4-core VM: async 979.0 RPS with a 105.4 ms p99 against sync-over-async 35.2 RPS with a 3530.7 ms p99 — 27.8x throughput and 33.5x lower p99 with zero infrastructure change. .Result blocks a pool thread for the whole wait and the pool grows by only one or two threads per second, so 96 of 100 requests queue for a thread rather than for the database. Matching it would take ~28 instances.

nodes.label: What stateless actually means
nodes.rationale: Not 'has no state' but 'no state that matters lives in the process'. Static dictionaries, in-memory semaphores, sessions, rate-limit counters, in-process job schedulers and SignalR groups all break at more than one instance; databases, row and advisory locks, distributed caches, queues with leader election and a SignalR Redis backplane survive. Spotting the same failure across unrelated technologies is what the interview question is really testing.

nodes.label: SignalR groups are per-process (ContentionHub)
nodes.rationale: This repo has the bug on purpose: at three replicas a client connected to instance 2 misses events published on instance 1, because SignalR groups live in process memory. Same class of failure as the in-memory lock in a different costume; the fix is a Redis backplane.

nodes.label: Idempotency keys for repeated operations
nodes.rationale: Concurrency safety does not make a repeated operation safe. Five retries applied five times leave a balance of 500 against an expected 900 — every retry individually correct and concurrency-safe, the customer still charged five times. The guarantee must come from a uniqueness constraint in the database: checking 'have I seen this key?' then inserting is the read-modify-write race wearing a different hat.

nodes.label: The costs of scaling out
nodes.rationale: Every replica multiplies database load; coordination gets slower (the distributed lock took ~2.6 s of total waiting where the in-process semaphore took ~8 ms — correctness across instances costs a round-trip per acquire); debugging needs correlation ids and aggregated logging; stateless costs infrastructure (Redis, backplane, queue with leader election). Vertical scaling is underrated: a bigger machine is often cheaper and always simpler.

nodes.label: Micro-benchmarking with BenchmarkDotNet
nodes.rationale: It handles JIT warmup, tiered compilation, outlier detection, statistical significance, allocation tracking and dead-code elimination — all of which hand-rolled Stopwatch code gets wrong below about a millisecond. Never point it at an HTTP endpoint: no concurrency, no pooling, no realistic contention, and it measures a network hop as if it were code. That is a category error worth being able to name.

nodes.label: Load testing the whole system
nodes.rationale: Benchmarking finds slow code; load testing finds slow systems. A method benchmarking at 50 ns can still produce an endpoint that collapses at 100 concurrent users, because the bottleneck was the connection pool, a lock, or thread-pool starvation — none of which exist in a single-threaded benchmark. Its cost is an environment resembling production; load testing an empty database tells you almost nothing.

nodes.label: A benchmark whose conditions you cannot state is a number, not evidence
nodes.rationale: The committed reports came from a 4-core shared cloud VM under a ShortRun job, so some Error values are the same order as the Mean. Fine for order-of-magnitude claims (11x, 1,857x), not for anything subtler — two results within 2x on this hardware are 'about the same'. Saying that is worth more in an interview than a table of impressive figures.

nodes.label: Dependency licence screening
nodes.rationale: BenchmarkDotNet is MIT and free commercially; NBomber moved to a paid commercial subscription (licence v3.0, September 2025) so the planned dependency was replaced with a small purpose-built harness in tests/Bank.LoadTests; k6 is AGPL-3.0 and its scripts are committed. Same reasoning that removed MediatR and FluentAssertions — a public teaching repo should not carry dependencies a reader cannot use at work.

nodes.label: Profile, benchmark, load test, measure in production
nodes.rationale: Do not benchmark what you have not proven is hot. Profile first (dotnet-trace, dotnet-counters), benchmark the hot method once identified, load test the system because the bottleneck usually is not the method, then measure in production. Most real problems are found at the last two steps; the satisfying numbers are at step 2, which is exactly why people over-invest there.

nodes.label: Lesson 11 — Interview questions with defensible answers
Concurrent collections protect their invariants, never yours
nodes.rationale: ConcurrentDictionary is thread-safe and does not help: TryGetValue, decide, TryUpdate is still a race. The same argument applies to ConcurrentQueue as an aggregation strategy in lesson 07.

nodes.label: lock vs Interlocked vs ReaderWriterLockSlim vs SemaphoreSlim cost
nodes.rationale: Interlocked is a single atomic instruction over a single variable — cheaper and cannot deadlock; lock gives mutual exclusion over a region. Measured uncontended against a plain increment: Interlocked 13.7x, lock 54.6x, ReaderWriterLockSlim 59.2x, SemaphoreSlim 117x.

nodes.label: Testing a race by making the interleaving a parameter
nodes.rationale: Not by running it a lot and hoping: an injected gate holds every actor after its read until all have read, so the lost update reproduces 100% of the time. Invariant tests then run free and assert only what must be true under any interleaving — money conserved, balance never negative — never who won, because that is asserting the scheduler. The concession to make in an interview is that this is test code in production, mitigated by compiling it out behind a flag; Coyote explores interleavings systematically rather than sampling.

nodes.label: k6 load scenarios
nodes.rationale: The k6 binary could not be downloaded in the environment this repo was built in, so the scripts are committed for local runs and the in-repo harness (tests/Bank.LoadTests) covers the same ground with no install.

nodes.label: k6 scenario: threadpool.js
nodes.rationale: Drives async against sync-over-async to reproduce thread-pool starvation over HTTP. Target overridable with -e BASE_URL.

nodes.label: k6 scenario: hot-account.js
nodes.rationale: Contention rather than CPU is the wall — one hot account versus load spread across many. Run against deploy/docker-compose.scale.yml it is what makes the in-process lock visibly fail, because requests through nginx land on different replicas holding different semaphores.

nodes.label: App shell template (topbar, nav, offline banner)
nodes.rationale: The shell polls API health and shows instanceId and core count; when the API is offline it explains that every page calls it and the UI computes nothing itself.

nodes.label: Home page — the mental model (tellers animation)
nodes.rationale: Two animated stages built off one clock so the comparison is fair: one teller juggling customers for concurrency, four counters for parallelism. Links onward to the Race lab.

nodes.label: Race lab page — timeline, silent losers, raw events
nodes.rationale: Renders per-actor lanes, a winners/silent-losers/refused stat grid, and a raw event table whose 'saw ver' column is the whole bug. The SignalR live feed is explicitly an accelerator, not the source of truth — the run response carries the full timeline anyway.

nodes.label: Compare page — every strategy on identical input
nodes.rationale: Runs all strategies against 5 actors withdrawing 100 from a balance of 100 with the race forced, so the only variable is the handler. Surfaces conflicts and waited side by side plus a scalesAcrossInstances badge, and repeats the which-one-when decision table.

nodes.label: Parallelism lab page — interest and fraud checks
nodes.rationale: Two sections: CPU-bound nightly interest computed six ways, and I/O-bound fraud checks with a throttle control that shows thread counts. The rule stated on the page: async is for waiting, Parallel is for working.

nodes.label: Scale lab page — three layers, deadlock and idempotency runners
nodes.rationale: Layer 1 charts the committed load-test RPS and p99 figures, layer 2 shows the 1-vs-3-instance strategy table, layer 3 has live buttons for the deadlock demo with and without lock ordering and the idempotency retry demo with and without a key.

nodes.label: Learn page — lesson map and flashcards
nodes.rationale: Mirrors the docs/lessons index and turns lesson 11's interview material into flashcards with an evidence line, plus the 'questions to ask them' list.
